An Assistant is a persistent, named, user-configured AI identity that the user creates once and returns to repeatedly. Editing an Assistant's configuration MUST preserve its canonical Assistant identity, appropriate history, valid conversations, Tasks/Runs, memories, permissions and artifacts unless the user explicitly chooses an operation whose documented effect is to remove or reset them. Assistant identity is separate from any individual conversation or task.

It supports creation, installation, import, execution, inspection, configuration, snapshots, cloning, networking, device integration, templates, developer workflows and recovery of supported virtual machines.

A VM remains a real provider-backed virtual machine. Mini Computer MUST NOT replace mature hypervisor functionality with a simplified simulation merely to obtain a uniform UI.
Built-in default provider: 9to1 VirtualBox fork
The built-in and default provider is a maintained 9to1 fork of the VirtualBox Platform Package source. Mini Computer MUST include this provider so a user can create and run supported VMs without first installing or connecting a third-party hypervisor.
The implementation MUST fork and maintain the latest appropriate VirtualBox source in accordance with the global donor/upstream contract and the applicable open-source licence/third-party licence obligations. The fork remains an auditable upstream-derived backend rather than an opaque binary dependency with no source provenance.
VirtualBox's mature virtual-machine creation, configuration, storage, networking, snapshot, cloning, import/export, console and management behaviours are mandatory donor-parity inputs where supported by the target architecture/platform.

Mini Computer exposes a canonical VirtualisationProvider interface. The built-in 9to1 VirtualBox fork is selected by default, while users may connect/install additional compatible providers such as QEMU, KVM, Windows hypervisor integrations or extension-contributed providers when supported.
Provider has stable ProviderID, type/vendor, version, connection/install state, supported hosts/guest architectures, acceleration capabilities, firmware/security capabilities, device/network/storage features, import/export formats, debug/serial support and Revision.
Connecting another provider does not change the canonical VM semantics automatically. Each VM records ProviderID, and provider migration/conversion is an explicit operation with a preview of unsupported/lossy features.
Provider-specific advanced controls remain accessible through typed provider configuration without leaking arbitrary implementation flags into the canonical cross-provider model.
Provider capability matrix
Every provider reports exact capability state rather than relying on feature hiding alone. Capabilities include supported guest architectures, hardware acceleration, nested virtualisation, snapshots, live snapshots, saved state, cloning, disk formats/controllers, BIOS/UEFI, Secure Boot, TPM, USB/device passthrough, shared folders, clipboard/drag-drop, virtual networking, graphics acceleration, multi-monitor, audio, serial/debug interfaces and live configuration changes.
A setting unsupported by the active provider/platform is marked Unsupported/Unavailable with a reason and remediation/alternative where applicable. Mini Computer MUST NOT accept a setting and silently ignore it.
Capabilities may depend on host architecture and current host configuration, so provider/version support and effective host support are distinct states.
Canonical VirtualMachine model
VirtualMachine has stable VMID, name, ProviderID, EnvironmentID, guest OS metadata, architecture, machine/chipset type, firmware/security configuration, CPU configuration, memory configuration, storage controllers/disks/media, network adapters, display/GPU, audio, USB/devices, integration policy, shared folders, clipboard/drag-drop policy, snapshot graph, template/source provenance, lifecycle state, Files/resource references and Revision.
Renaming, moving in UI or changing provider display labels MUST NOT alter VMID. Provider-internal identifiers are retained as mappings rather than becoming the only canonical identity.
VM configuration is versioned and migratable. Unsupported/unknown future configuration is preserved/rejected explicitly rather than silently dropped.

Canonical lifecycle states include at least PoweredOff, Starting, Running, Pausing, Paused, SavingState, Saved, Resuming, ShuttingDown, Stopping, Crashed, Disconnected/ViewerUnavailable and ProviderUnavailable where distinct.
Viewer state and VM state are separate. Closing or losing a viewer MUST NOT cause the UI to report PoweredOff if the VM remains running.
Lifecycle transitions are driven by verified provider state. Mini Computer MUST NOT report Start/Shutdown/Save successful until the provider confirms the resulting state or the operation explicitly remains Pending.

Every supported VM can expose Open in Terminal for guest shell/SSH where configured, serial console, debug console or provider-supported command channel. This uses the shared Terminal engine.
Terminal creates/attaches an EnvironmentID tied to VMID/provider/guest channel and visibly identifies the VM so commands cannot be mistaken for host commands.
Closing Terminal does not power off the VM; VM lifecycle remains owned by Mini Computer.
Dev integration and Run target
Dev uses Mini Computer as the canonical VM runtime for projects whose RunConfiguration targets a VM. Dev MUST NOT maintain a parallel private hypervisor implementation.
For OS/kernel projects, Run can execute Build → package boot artifact → obtain/start configured Mini Computer VM → attach disk/ISO/EFI/kernel artifact → boot → expose viewer/serial/debug state.
Run configuration references stable VM/template/provider identities and can declare reset/snapshot/discard policy for repeatable development.
Ephemeral development VMs
Dev/CI can request ephemeral VMs derived from templates/snapshots for isolated testing. Policy can specify discard after success, preserve on failure, always preserve or snapshot-before-run.
Ephemeral instances receive unique VMID/runtime identity even when created from the same template and do not mutate the reusable template/base unintentionally.
Cleanup waits until logs/artifacts/checks referencing the ephemeral environment are retained or explicitly discarded.
OS/kernel debugging integration
Mini Computer exposes provider-supported serial ports/consoles, debug stubs, reset/power control, boot logs and low-level debug channels through typed capabilities.
Dev owns source-level debugger UI such as breakpoints, symbols, registers/memory/disassembly mapping where supported; Mini Computer supplies the VM/provider channel and exact machine state.
Debug integration records the source VM/revision/artifact mapping so Dev cannot accidentally attach symbols from an unrelated build.
Headless operation
VMs may run without an open viewer. Closing Mini Computer follows explicit/configured behaviour such as Keep running, Save state or Ask; it does not inherently terminate a VM.
A background/service component owns provider sessions that must survive the UI process. Reopening Mini Computer discovers/reattaches to existing provider VMs instead of creating duplicates.

requirements.requirement: Assistant tool efficiency preserves quality, scope and safe steering

sources.quote:
8. Tool-call optimisation and batching
Optimise time and cost to a verified result, not tool-call volume. Apply to all agents, including ordinary chat models performing agentic work, Assistants, Specialists and delegated workers. Default to: probe when uncertain → plan the whole work unit → batch execute → verify → repair. Do not insert fresh model reasoning between predictable individual operations.


Probe only when needed — Read the relevant tool contract and reuse verified knowledge for the same tool/version/environment. If behaviour is unfamiliar or uncertain, run a minimal, reversible representative test: one object, or the smallest batch needed to check bulk behaviour. Inspect actual units, axes, placement, scale, rotation, asset references and returned IDs as applicable. Delete only the test objects using their recorded IDs and confirm cleanup before production work. Prefer safe staging or dry-run support where available. Repeat probes only when relevant assumptions change; a successful small probe does not establish large-batch capacity.


Plan the whole work unit — Design the complete building, track or other coherent deliverable before executing its repetitive operations. Prepare a deterministic operation manifest containing the assets, transforms/parameters, dependencies, expected outputs and checks; validate it before submission. Generate repetitive data programmatically where supported instead of individually reasoning through each item. Revise the plan when new evidence, failures or user steering require it, not after every successful operation.


Batch execution — Submit the complete validated work unit in one supported bulk call when safe. Otherwise use bounded chunks, or a supported authorised script/executor that runs the planned calls without a model turn per item. Do not invent a bulk endpoint or assume every MCP supports batching. Where no suitable executor exists, use the available calls efficiently and disclose the constraint rather than claiming a batch occurred. Preserve dependency ordering; parallelise only independent operations that the service can safely process.


Adaptive limits — Choose batch size from known or measured payload, timeout, rate, memory, recovery and responsiveness limits. Start conservatively when capacity is unknown, increase after successful observations and reduce or change approach after failures. Do not jump from one successful test object to 50,000 untested placements. Keep execution interruptible at supported safe boundaries so steering, pause and cancellation remain effective. Batching never expands permissions or bypasses per-action approval requirements.


Verify and recover — Check results after each logical batch or bounded chunk using actual state readback and appropriate visual inspection; verify the assembled result against the manifest and acceptance criteria. For a map, inspect the actual scene from useful views and test relevant traversal/collision behaviour, not merely the reported object count. A successful tool response or sampled visual check alone does not verify the whole deliverable. Repair affected items and rerun relevant checks. Track per-item outcomes and created IDs; after partial failure or timeout, reconcile actual state before retrying, preserve successful work and avoid duplicates. Roll back only identified task-owned changes where safe, never unrelated user work.


Avoid redundant overhead — Reuse current schemas, asset lookups and unchanged results; refresh when invalidated or freshness matters. Batch related reads, request only needed fields and keep large manifests/logs outside repeated model context, with concise summaries and retrievable evidence. Avoid per-object screenshots, explanations, schema rediscovery and busy polling when batch-level evidence suffices. Record real batch/checkpoint progress in the existing dashboard without turning every object into a checkpoint. Efficiency must never weaken quality, required checks or the final verification gate.

Tool-efficiency release checks: demonstrate unfamiliar-tool probing and cleanup, reuse of valid tool knowledge, whole-unit planning, supported batching/chunking without per-object replanning, visual and functional verification, partial-failure recovery without duplicates, and steering at safe boundaries. Compare elapsed time, model turns and tool round trips with a per-item baseline on the same representative task and acceptance tests; efficiency gains must preserve output quality and verification coverage.

sources.quote:
An Assistant is a persistent, named, user-configured AI identity that the user creates once and returns to repeatedly. It is substantially more than a saved prompt, renamed chat, system-prompt textbox, template, one-off agentic Task, Space or delegated subagent. The same Assistant identity can span multiple conversations, Tasks/Runs, projects, scheduled work, memories/context where permitted, artifacts, checkpoints and applicable Mini Computer state. Starting a new conversation does not create a new Assistant, and delegating a worker does not create another personal Assistant.
The intended experience is: “this is my persistent AI assistant that knows its configured role, can use authorised tools and resources, can continue real work over time, and can proactively help when I have enabled that behaviour” — not “this is a chat with a long system prompt.”
Assistant configuration and identity
Each Assistant MUST have a persistent editable configuration and stable identity. Where applicable the configuration includes name, icon/avatar, description, purpose/role, instructions/personality, preferred model or model policy, reasoning/model-routing preferences, allowed tools, connected apps/services, authorised files/projects/knowledge sources, memory behaviour, computer-use permissions, Mini Computer configuration, Dev/project access, proactive-behaviour settings, notification/check-in preferences, schedules/Automations, voice/multimodal preferences and resource/usage limits. These settings must be exposed through polished product UI rather than relying primarily on raw prompt/config files.
Editing an Assistant's configuration MUST preserve its canonical Assistant identity, appropriate history, valid conversations, Tasks/Runs, memories, permissions and artifacts unless the user explicitly chooses an operation whose documented effect is to remove or reset them. Assistant identity is separate from any individual conversation or task.

Smoke verification MUST exercise the actual packaged app, including launch, configured Assistant selection/creation as applicable, genuine conversation, persistence/reopen, shared Spaces-runtime integration, Dev handoff, permissions, at least one genuine authorised development action, steering and clean close/reopen. Extensive verification must then cover the complete Agentic Update contracts, including durable Task/Run persistence, recovery, coordinated workers, Task Dashboard/widget integration, permission enforcement, computer-use notice/control where applicable, Mini Computer operation where applicable, failed-action recovery without duplicated effects, checkpoint/artifact history, correct Assistant identity after restart and supported cross-device/platform behaviour.

Web Apps
Cakemods.com MUST host a web version of every 9-1 Workspace/AI product that is not explicitly listed as web-exempt. Web surfaces MUST share the same CAKE ID identity, canonical artifact formats, domain APIs, permission model and underlying server-side entities as desktop equivalents. Browser-specific UI/layout MAY differ, but it MUST NOT create a separate incompatible product model.




The default rule is to provide a web version whenever the product’s core value can sensibly work in a browser. Browser-specific capability limits are acceptable when they are explicit and the useful core product remains intact; a single desktop-only feature is not by itself a reason to omit an otherwise useful web app.

Use the existing canonical task/run, Automations, permissions, activity, artifact, generative-UI and tab services rather than competing stores. Expose equivalent typed API actions for dashboard operations. Apply existing CUI, accessibility, privacy, recovery and cross-device requirements.
